\title{Large Language Models for Software Requirements\\Classification:
       Cross-Dataset Generalization and Cost-Efficiency}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Fatma El-Zahraa Samir, Khaled T. Wassif, and Lamia AbouZeid}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Faculty of Computers and Artificial Intelligence},
\textit{Cairo University}, Giza, Egypt\\
fatmaelzahraasamirabdelfattah@gmail.com}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Several recent studies report that prompted large language models (LLMs) match
or exceed fine-tuned transformer baselines on software requirements
classification, and some of them conclude that labelled training data is no
longer needed for the task. Those results are almost always obtained
in-distribution, with training data or few-shot exemplars drawn from the same
corpus that supplies the test items, and they rarely report what the technique
costs to run. This paper re-examines the comparison after repairing both
omissions. Fine-tuned encoders and prompted LLMs of three access tiers classify
the same requirements from two public corpora, under the same tasks and the same
scoring rule, at three levels of distribution shift: within one corpus, across
held-out projects, and across an independently annotated corpus. Every
encoder--LLM comparison is paired on identical items and corrected for
multiplicity as one test family, and inference cost is measured per model from
the same runs that produced the predictions. The ranking of the two approaches
is not stable across those levels. Within a corpus the fine-tuned encoders are
ahead and are never significantly beaten; once the test corpus is annotated by
someone else the ordering reverses and the prompted models are ahead in most
comparisons. The reason is not that the transferred encoder fails to recognise
the vocabulary of the new corpus but that it carries the class balance of the
corpus it was trained on, and the prompted models turn out to have the same
weakness for a different reason: their class balance is set by the wording of
the instruction, and changing that wording moves it. Encoders remain an order of
magnitude cheaper per item and recover their one-off training cost within a few
hundred classifications. The practical implication is that the evaluation regime
belongs in the claim: a result obtained in-distribution does not predict the
ranking under a change of corpus, and can reverse it.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
requirements classification, large language models, fine-tuning, generalisation,
distribution shift, empirical software engineering, cost-efficiency
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%% ===========================================================================

Requirements classification assigns natural-language requirement statements to
categories such as functional (FR) versus non-functional (NFR), or
security-relevant versus not. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 defines requirements and their
attributes for the whole life cycle~\cite{iso29148}, and classification is one
of the first analytical steps performed once requirements have been elicited.
Getting it right supports early risk identification and architectural choice;
getting it wrong propagates downstream as rework~\cite{clelandhuang2007}. Two
decades of automation have moved the task from weighted indicator
terms~\cite{clelandhuang2007}, through supervised learning on engineered
features~\cite{kurtanovic2017,dalpiaz2019}, to fine-tuned
transformers~\cite{hey2020norbert} and, since 2024, to prompted generative
LLMs~\cite{elhajjami2024,binkhonain2025,alhoshan2025,tang2025,levy2026}. A
systematic mapping of AI techniques applied to the task documents the same
progression and the datasets it has relied on~\cite{kaur2024}.

It is worth being precise about what this recent work claims. No study we are
aware of states that requirements classification is solved. What several studies
report is parity or better between prompting and supervision on the corpora they
use: Binkhonain and Alfayaz find that few-shot prompting matches or exceeds a
fine-tuned transformer and conclude that prompting is a viable alternative where
labelled data is scarce~\cite{binkhonain2025}; Tang et al.\ report an 8\,B open
model passing a fine-tuned baseline on PROMISE~\cite{tang2025}; and Alhoshan et
al.\ report that generative models perform the task competitively without
task-specific training~\cite{alhoshan2025}, extending earlier evidence that
zero-shot embedding methods already made labelled data non-essential in some
settings~\cite{alhoshan2023}. Together these results make ``prompting can
replace fine-tuning'' a reasonable reading of the state of the art, and it is
that reading, rather than any individual paper's claim, that this study tests.

The reading rests on a measurement convention. Almost every published result is
obtained in-distribution: the model is fine-tuned, or its few-shot exemplars are
selected, on the same corpus that then supplies the test items. Where prior work
reports improved generalisability, it usually means transfer across \emph{tasks}
on the same corpora rather than to unseen projects or an independently produced
dataset~\cite{binkhonain2025}---the property the field's own transfer-learning
baseline warned about, since NoRBERT was motivated by classifiers over-fitting
project-specific wording~\cite{hey2020norbert}. A second omission compounds the
first: inference cost, latency and model size are seldom quantified, although
they decide whether a technique can be adopted without a commercial API budget.

This paper asks what happens to the comparison when both omissions are repaired.
We hold the corpus, the items, the label sets and the scoring rule fixed, and
vary only the distribution shift between what a model was fitted on and what it
is scored on. Our contributions are:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A paired, multiplicity-controlled benchmark} of twelve
configurations---four fine-tuned encoder variants and eight prompted LLMs across
local, hosted and commercial access tiers---over three tasks, two corpora and
three evaluation regimes, scored once under one strict protocol, with all
encoder--LLM tests corrected as a single family
(Sections~\ref{sec:design} and~\ref{sec:results}).
\item \textbf{Evidence that the ranking depends on the regime.} Within a corpus
the encoders are ahead and are never significantly beaten; across corpora the
same comparisons reverse (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}).
\item \textbf{A diagnosis rather than a gap.} The collapse under corpus change is
consistent with a shift in class balance rather than with unfamiliar vocabulary,
and the prompted models have the same defect from another source: their
predicted class balance is set by the wording of the instruction
(Sections~\ref{sec:rq2} and~\ref{sec:prior}).
\item \textbf{A measured accuracy--cost comparison}, with the price of each
configuration derived from the same runs that produced its predictions, and the
compute-priced and token-priced tiers reported separately
(Section~\ref{sec:rq3}).
\end{enumerate}

Three research questions organise the study. \textbf{RQ1}: how do open and
commercial LLMs compare with fine-tuned encoders when both are evaluated within
one corpus? \textbf{RQ2}: how much performance is lost under cross-project and
cross-dataset evaluation, and does the loss differ between the two model
families? \textbf{RQ3}: what is the accuracy-versus-cost trade-off, and what is
the cheapest freely available option that is good enough?

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work and the Evaluation Gap}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{From indicator terms to prompting}
Automated requirements classification has passed through four overlapping
phases. Rule-based work established the task and produced the PROMISE NFR
collection~\cite{clelandhuang2007}. Classical supervised learning followed, with
SVMs separating FRs from NFRs~\cite{kurtanovic2017} and interpretable variants
combining dependency parsing with feature attribution~\cite{dalpiaz2019}; deep
models removed much of the feature engineering but needed more
data~\cite{sonawane2024}. Transfer learning then reset the state of the art:
NoRBERT fine-tunes BERT and reports \Fm{} in the mid nineties on the PROMISE
categories~\cite{hey2020norbert}, a pattern the systematic mapping of Kaur and
Kaur later confirmed across the published literature~\cite{kaur2024}. Zero-shot
sentence-embedding methods then showed that labelled data was not strictly
necessary~\cite{alhoshan2023}, and prompted generative LLMs now dominate recent
work.

\subsection{Recent LLM studies (2024--2026)}
El-Hajjami et al.~\cite{elhajjami2024} compared SVM and LSTM against GPT-3.5 and
GPT-4 over five datasets and found no single best technique; Peer et
al.~\cite{peer2024} embedded LLM classification in a model-based systems
engineering workflow. Binkhonain and Alfayaz~\cite{binkhonain2025} report the
study closest to ours: five LLMs under four prompting strategies over three
tasks on PROMISE and SecReq, benchmarked against a fine-tuned transformer that
few-shot prompting matches or exceeds. Alhoshan et al.~\cite{alhoshan2025} ran
more than 400 experiments over three open generative models, and Tang et
al.~\cite{tang2025} identified an over-prompting effect in which additional
in-context examples degrade accuracy on PROMISE and PURE~\cite{ferrari2017pure},
while a TF--IDF exemplar selector pushes an 8\,B open model past the fine-tuned
baseline. Chaudhary et al.~\cite{chaudhary2025} extended the task to noisy
app-store reviews, Vasudevan et al.~\cite{vasudevan2026} compared fine-tuned
BERT and RoBERTa against GPT-4o, and Levy et al.~\cite{levy2026} benchmarked
three current models against expert judgment on \pex{}.

\subsection{What this literature does not measure}
\label{sec:gap}
Table~\ref{tab:coverage} summarises the evaluation coverage of these studies
along the axes that matter for adoption, and three patterns recur.
\emph{First}, evaluation is in-distribution: the same corpus supplies the
training data or the few-shot exemplars and the test items. Only the app-review
study~\cite{chaudhary2025} tests genuinely different text, and it reports
markedly lower precision on several categories---a signal the literature has not
followed up. \emph{Second}, cost is not a reported dimension, even in the
studies that use open models~\cite{alhoshan2025,tang2025}. \emph{Third}, the
same two or three small, ageing, public corpora underlie nearly every result, so
contamination of LLM pre-training data is a threat that is acknowledged but not
addressed~\cite{sainz2023}.

These gaps interact. If in-distribution parity is what motivates replacing
supervision with prompting, and is also what corpus reuse and contamination
would produce spuriously, then the comparison that would settle the question has
not been run. This study runs it: the same models, items and scoring rule,
evaluated at three levels of distribution shift, with inference cost measured
alongside accuracy.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Study Design}
\label{sec:design}
%% ===========================================================================

The study is a controlled benchmark. Twelve model configurations classify the
same requirements, under the same tasks, against the same frozen splits, scored
by one rule, so every comparison we report is paired on identical items.
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the design: one data and scoring path shared by both
model families, and three evaluation regimes of increasing distribution shift.
The pipeline runs as seven stages, each writing a content-hashed artefact that
the next consumes; every number in Section~\ref{sec:results} is read back from
those artefacts by the scripts that typeset the tables and figures.

\input{figures/fig_architecture}

\subsection{Data preparation}
\label{sec:data}
Two public corpora are used. \pex{}~\cite{lima2019}, an expanded release of the
PROMISE NFR collection, contributes 969 requirements from 47 projects, each
labelled FR or NFR and, when NFR, with one of eleven quality sub-types.
SecReq~\cite{knauss2011} contributes 510 sentences from three industrial
security specifications, each labelled security-relevant or not.

Preparation proceeds in four steps, implemented once in the first pipeline
stage. \emph{(i)~Normalisation:} texts are whitespace- and encoding-normalised,
and label strings are mapped onto one controlled vocabulary so that the two
corpora express the security concept identically. \emph{(ii)~De-duplication:}
exact duplicate texts are removed---67 rows, all of them within a corpus rather
than across the two---leaving 1{,}412 requirements in 50 project groups
(Table~\ref{tab:corpus}). \emph{(iii)~Split generation:} the fourteen split
families used by the three regimes are generated once with seed 42 and stored,
keyed by requirement identifiers pinned to the SHA-256 hash of each source file.
Because grouped-fold membership depends on the library version that produced
it~\cite{pedregosa2011}, the split file is consumed by later stages and never
regenerated. \emph{(iv)~Frame construction:} each task defines the set of items
it is evaluated on, as described below.

Two properties of the result matter for the rest of the paper. The first is a
difference in class balance: security requirements are 12.9\% of \pex{} but
39.9\% of SecReq, a roughly threefold difference in prevalence for a concept
both corpora annotate independently, and the cross-dataset regime is built on
that contrast. The second is that the security label reaches the two corpora by
different routes. In \pex{} it is derived from the security sub-class of the NFR
taxonomy, so every \pex{} item labelled security is also labelled NFR and none
of the 444 FRs is labelled security; in SecReq it is applied to any
security-relevant sentence, with no FR/NFR annotation at all. The cross-dataset
regime therefore carries a definitional shift alongside the distributional one,
and we return to this in the threats to validity.

\subsection{Tasks, label sets, and why they are not staged}
\label{sec:tasks}
Three task families are defined over the unified corpus.
\emph{Binary FR/NFR} uses the native \pex{} labels over all 968 \pex{} items.
\emph{Binary security} is native in SecReq and derived in \pex{} from the
security sub-class, which gives the same task on two independently produced
corpora. \emph{NFR sub-type} classification uses the eleven-class taxonomy of
Cleland-Huang et al.~\cite{clelandhuang2007}, whose categories align with the
ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics~\cite{iso25010}.

The three tasks are evaluated independently. There is no cascade: the security
classifier is not shown the output of the FR/NFR classifier, and every item is
presented to it directly, including the 444 \pex{} items labelled FR. We state
this because the \pex{} \emph{annotation} is hierarchical---security is a
sub-class of NFR---so it would be easy to assume the \emph{pipeline} is
hierarchical too. It is not, and deliberately so: a staged design would make the
security score depend on the FR/NFR classifier's errors, and would have no
counterpart in SecReq, where no FR/NFR labels exist. Keeping the tasks flat is
what makes the security task comparable across the two corpora.

Several sub-type classes have single-digit support in \pex{}, so the sub-type
task is evaluated at three granularities: the full eleven classes (524 items),
the six most frequent (433) and the four most frequent (353). For a fine-tuned
encoder the label set determines the size of the classification head and the
model is re-trained for each granularity. For a prompted model there is no head
to resize and no training at all, so it is fair to ask what top-4 and top-6
mean. They change three things. The candidate labels are enumerated inside the
prompt itself, so at top-4 the model is offered four labels and at all-11
eleven. The evaluation frame changes: an item enters the top-4 frame only if its
true label is one of those four. And \Fm{} is computed over the full declared
label set of the variant, so a model is penalised for every declared class it
never predicts, and that denominator grows with granularity. Granularity is a
property of the question and of the scoring rather than of the model weights,
and it is therefore measurable for prompted and fine-tuned models alike.

\subsection{Evaluation regimes}
Fourteen frozen split families, comprising 107 folds, implement three regimes of
increasing distribution shift.
\textbf{In-domain} is stratified 5-fold cross-validation within one corpus. This
is the in-distribution setting that prior work reports.
\textbf{Cross-project} uses grouped folds that hold out entire unseen project
groups, plus a leave-one-project-out variant over the 47 \pex{} projects.
\textbf{Cross-dataset} fits on the security task of one corpus and tests on the
other, in both directions: identical label sets, different annotation
provenance.

The asymmetry between the two model families is the analytical lever. Encoders
are re-fitted at every regime on that regime's training folds; prompted models
have no training distribution, so their scores cannot change with the regime,
which is why the same score appears in every regime column of
Table~\ref{tab:main}. Every requirement is a test item exactly once within each
encoder family, so the encoders' stored predictions cover the corpus. The
prompted models answer stratified samples of the same items---300 per binary
cell and 200 per sub-type cell, allocated in proportion to the class prior with
a floor of ten per class---and the six local models additionally answer the full
evaluation frames. Every encoder--LLM comparison is paired on identical
requirements, aligned by identifier rather than by position.

\subsection{The two model families, and why they are compared}
\label{sec:families}
Table~\ref{tab:models} lists the twelve configurations. The comparison is
between two architectures, and the difference is not incidental to the question.

A fine-tuned encoder is a bidirectional, encoder-only transformer pre-trained
with masked language modelling and then adapted by supervised training of a
classification head over the pooled sentence representation. Both the decision
boundary and the class prior are learned from the labelled training folds. A
prompted LLM is a decoder-only autoregressive model that has not been adapted to
the task at all: it receives the label vocabulary as text, produces the answer
as generated tokens, and its implicit class prior comes from pre-training and
from the instruction rather than from any corpus of requirements.

That contrast is what makes the comparison informative, because the two families
should respond differently to distribution shift precisely by acquiring their
class prior from different places---and Section~\ref{sec:prior} shows that they
do. Prior work has argued that architectural choice affects requirements
classification results~\cite{vasudevan2026}, so we treat architecture as a
declared property rather than a nuisance variable: Table~\ref{tab:models}
records the family, parameter count and access tier of every model, and all
results are reported per configuration.

We fine-tune \texttt{bert-base-uncased}~\cite{devlin2019} and
\texttt{roberta-base}~\cite{liu2019} with a classification head (AdamW,
lr $2\times10^{-5}$, batch 16, max length 128, linear decay without warmup, full
precision; 3 epochs on the binary tasks, 10 on the sub-types), each with
inverse-frequency class weighting in the loss, plus an unweighted control on the
security task. The local tier runs six instruction-tuned models of 2.6--8.0\,B
parameters on a single free-tier NVIDIA T4 under 4-bit NF4
quantisation~\cite{dettmers2023}. The hosted tier accesses Llama-3.3-70B and the
commercial tier Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, both through free API tiers. A ninth
prompted model was attempted and failed the reportability gate defined below;
its predictions remain in the raw store but enter no table.

\subsection{Prompt design and what it is meant to control}
\label{sec:prompt}
Each prompted model answers a fixed instruction that names the task, enumerates
the label vocabulary and requires exactly one word in reply, sent as a single
user message (Fig.~\ref{fig:prompt}). Decoding is greedy---temperature $0$, at
most twelve new tokens---so the only stochastic element is item sampling.

Fixing the instruction needs justifying, because a different wording could give
a different result. Three points define what the choice does and does not claim.

\emph{Where the wording comes from.} The template follows the zero-shot format
used in the LLM requirements-classification studies we compare
against~\cite{binkhonain2025,alhoshan2025,tang2025}: a short task statement, an
explicit list of permitted labels, and an instruction to answer with the label
alone. We did not tune it against the test items. A conventional instruction
keeps the comparison with prior work interpretable; a tuned one would not.

\emph{We do not claim it is the best prompt.} Almost certainly it is not. What
the design requires is a \emph{fixed} instruction, so that the only quantity
varying across the three regimes is the distribution shift. If the prompt were
re-optimised per regime, a difference between regimes could no longer be
attributed to the shift. The fixed prompt is a control, not a recommendation.

\emph{What the wording is worth is measured, not assumed.} Two sub-studies vary
one factor at a time. The first re-runs two models over three phrasings of the
same question---\emph{base}, \emph{terse} and \emph{verbose}---with the answer
contract held identical; Table~\ref{tab:prompt} reports all nine paired cells.
Its last column gives the gain an oracle would obtain by picking the best of the
three wordings for each cell: a median of $+0.003$ \Fm{} and a maximum of
$+0.036$, far smaller than the differences this paper's conclusions rest on.
Picking that wording would in any case need labelled data from the target
corpus, which is the resource prompting is meant to do without. The second
sub-study is a few-shot ladder ($k \in \{2,4,8\}$ in total on the binary tasks,
$k \in \{1,2\}$ per class on the sub-types) with deterministic, class-balanced
exemplars carved out of the corpus \emph{before} the evaluation frames are
formed, so an exemplar is never also a test item. The hosted and commercial
tiers run zero-shot only, under provider rate limits.

\subsection{Parsing, metrics, and how to read them}
\label{sec:metrics}
Outputs are parsed by a strict, word-boundary-aware rule: a leading label wins;
otherwise exactly one label named anywhere in the reply wins; a reply naming
both labels or neither is unparseable and is scored as wrong. This is harsher
than the lenient protocols common in prior work, and it matches deployment,
where an unusable answer is not a free pass. The same rule is applied at
generation time and again in an idempotent repair pass over the archived raw
outputs, so stored and scored predictions cannot diverge.

Four kinds of quantity are reported, and because they are easy to confuse we
state what each one is. \emph{Macro-F1} is the unweighted mean of the per-class
F1 scores over the full declared label set of the task variant; it is the
primary metric because it does not let a model score well by ignoring a rare
class, and the majority-class baseline in the last row of Table~\ref{tab:main}
gives every score a floor to be read against. \emph{Relative loss}
($\Delta\%$ in Table~\ref{tab:loss}) is the share of a configuration's own
in-domain macro-F1 lost in a shifted regime, on the same items; it is defined
only for the encoders, since only they have an in-domain fit to lose.
\emph{Predicted class share} is the fraction of test items a model assigns to a
class. It is not an accuracy: it is what the model takes the class balance to
be, read against the true prevalence in the same items. It and relative loss are
both percentages, so Section~\ref{sec:rq2} names the class and the corpus each
time one is used. \emph{Test counts} are numbers of statistical comparisons, not
of items: each unit is one exact McNemar test between one encoder configuration
and one prompted model in one cell.

Uncertainty uses a stratified bootstrap~\cite{efron1993}: 2{,}000 resamples
drawn within each true class (seed 42), so no resample can lose a rare class.
Encoder--LLM comparisons use the exact two-sided McNemar test on paired
disagreements~\cite{mcnemar1947,dietterich1998}; all 260 are corrected as one
family under both Holm~\cite{holm1979} and
Benjamini--Hochberg~\cite{benjamini1995} at $\alpha = 0.05$, with verdicts keyed
on the BH-adjusted $p$ (175 significant before correction, 170 after BH, 131
after Holm). A cell---one model, task, dataset and regime---is reported only if
every class has at least 5 test items, the cell holds at least 40 items, and the
model parsed at least 50\% of its responses; 6 of 87 cells fail this gate and are
excluded rather than imputed. The store holds 76{,}115 predictions: 24{,}280 from
the encoders, 35{,}049 prompted binary and 16{,}786 prompted sub-type.

\subsection{Cost model}
\label{sec:costmodel}
Every prediction row records input and output token counts, wall-clock latency
and, for the encoders, training time. Cost is then computed from those recorded
quantities rather than estimated afterwards, and the basis differs by tier
because the two kinds of model are billed differently.

\emph{Models that run on our own hardware are priced on compute.} That covers
the fine-tuned encoders and all six local open-weight models: they are free to
download and carry no licence fee, so the only thing to charge for is the
machine time they consume. We price it as an imputed rental of the benchmark
GPU---an AWS \texttt{g4dn.xlarge} with one NVIDIA T4, at the published
on-demand list rate for \texttt{us-east-1} of \$0.5260 per hour, recorded in
the pipeline manifest with the date it was checked. That is a list price for
hardware, not a market price for the model, and it assumes sequential unbatched
inference; the stored sensitivity table reports the same costs at the spot rate
(\$0.3162/h) and at batch sizes 8 and 32, which cut the local figures by roughly
an order of magnitude.

\emph{Models behind an API are priced on tokens}, at the provider's published
list rate per million input and output tokens---\$0.25/\$1.50 for Gemini 3.1
Flash-Lite and \$0.59/\$0.79 for Llama-3.3-70B, taken from the providers' public
rate cards in August 2026 and frozen into every prediction row at generation
time, so a later price change cannot alter a stored result. Both models were in
fact run on free tiers; the list rate is what the same volume would have cost.

Neither basis is a fixed property of the technique, and cost should be expected
to move with model size and capability. Within the compute-priced tier it does:
over the ten locally executed configurations, cost per item rises with parameter
count (Spearman $\rho = 0.85$). That is why Table~\ref{tab:cost} puts parameter
counts next to prices and why Section~\ref{sec:rq3} states the comparison as a
ratio between tiers rather than an absolute price that would date. The ordering
is not perfectly monotonic in size, because a locally run model is charged for
the wall-clock time it occupies the GPU, and a model that emits longer replies
pays for them at equal size.

Encoder cost separates the one-off fine-tuning cost $C_0$ from the marginal
per-item cost $c_{\text{enc}}$, which gives a break-even volume against any
prompted alternative
\begin{equation}
N^{\star} \;=\; \frac{C_0}{c_{\text{alt}} - c_{\text{enc}}} .
\label{eq:breakeven}
\end{equation}
Because free-tier latency is dominated by provider-side queueing, wall-clock
projections use per-request median latency, with the queue-inflated mean
reported separately.

priced. USD/1k is the inference cost of 1{,}000 classifications; where a tier
holds several models the range spans their per-model medians. ``Train'' is the
one-off fine-tuning cost of a deployable model. Rates are those of
Section~\ref{sec:costmodel}.}
\label{tab:cost}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
%% ===========================================================================

Table~\ref{tab:main} is the paper's single results table. It carries all twelve
configurations, the six task-by-corpus cells and every regime each cell
supports, so encoders and prompted models are read off the same rows and
columns. The encoders have one score per regime because they are re-fitted at
each; a prompted model has one score per cell, written across the regime columns
it spans, because a model that consumes no training data cannot score
differently when the training data changes.

\label{tab:main}

\subsection{RQ1: within one corpus, supervision is still ahead}
Reading the \ID{} columns of Table~\ref{tab:main}, fine-tuned encoders hold the
best score in five of the six cells. Class-weighted BERT leads on FR/NFR and on
\pex{} security, and class-weighted RoBERTa leads on all three sub-type
granularities. The exception is SecReq security, where 4-bit Qwen2.5-7B posts
the better point estimate (0.846 against 0.836), a lead that does not reach
significance (exact McNemar $p = 0.696$; BH-adjusted $0.774$).

Three observations qualify that ranking. Scale does not order the results: the
2.6\,B Gemma-2-2B beats the hosted 70\,B model on \pex{} security, and the small
open models fall well below the encoders on FR/NFR while staying competitive on
security. The encoder advantage widens as the label set grows---from $+0.014$ on
top-4 and $+0.013$ on top-6 to $+0.095$ on all-11 over the best prompted
model---as one would expect if supervision mainly buys the long tail of rare
classes. Cell sizes differ, so the top-4 ranking was recomputed on the 59 items
every model answered; the best encoder still leads there by $+0.036$ (0.966
against 0.930), so the ordering is not an artefact of coverage. Every reportable
model clears its majority-class baseline.

The paired tests make the in-domain verdict precise. Of the 106 in-domain
encoder-versus-LLM comparisons, the encoder wins 67, 39 are inconclusive, and
none is lost (Fig.~\ref{fig:inversion}\,(b)).

\subsection{RQ2: the ranking reverses under distribution shift}
\label{sec:rq2}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_inversion.pdf}
\caption{(a) Security classification on \pex{}; all three bars are scored on the
same 968 items at every regime. The encoders are re-fitted at each regime; the
third bar is the median of the eight prompted models, with the whisker spanning
their range, and it is flat because those models are never fitted. The red
annotations are BERT's relative loss against its own in-domain score. (b) The
260 paired encoder-versus-LLM comparisons, grouped by the regime the encoder was
evaluated under. Each unit on the axis is one exact McNemar test, not one
requirement.}
\label{fig:inversion}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:loss} lists every measured transfer for the encoders, and
Fig.~\ref{fig:inversion} shows the comparison against the prompted models.

\textbf{Cross-project transfer is survivable.} Holding out unseen projects costs
the encoders between 3\% and 12\% of their in-domain \Fm{} on \pex{}, and up to
30\% on the much smaller SecReq, whose three project groups make a held-out group
a third of the corpus. The encoders remain ahead or tied in 76 of the 90 paired
tests at this regime---the degradation NoRBERT
anticipated~\cite{hey2020norbert}: real, but moderate.

\textbf{Cross-dataset transfer reverses the ranking.} The class-weighted BERT
that scores 0.923 on \pex{} security falls to 0.528 on the same items once its
training corpus is swapped for SecReq. That is a loss of 42.8\% of its in-domain
macro-F1, and it is the largest loss in the study; it belongs to the
cross-dataset regime, and should not be read against the cross-project losses in
the previous paragraph, whose maximum is 29.6\%. RoBERTa is more robust
($0.902 \rightarrow 0.698$, a loss of 23\%) and the reverse direction milder
still (16--17\%). The prompted models, having nothing to re-fit, move only with
the difficulty of the corpus. Over the 64 cross-dataset comparisons the prompted
models win 48 and the encoders 3; the in-domain tally of 67--39--0 becomes
3--13--48, on the same twelve models and the same scorer.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Relative loss under shift for the four fine-tuned encoders. $\Delta\%$
is the share of that configuration's own in-domain \Fm{} lost in the shifted
regime, on the same items. Prompted models are absent because they have no
in-domain fit to lose; their scores are in Table~\ref{tab:main}. Cross-dataset
applies only to the security task, the one both corpora annotate.}
\label{tab:loss}
\centering
\footnotesize
\input{tables/tab_loss}
\end{table}

\textbf{Corpus-level averages hide per-project failure.} On the
leave-one-project-out variant of FR/NFR, over the 37 projects with comparable
coverage, every configuration---encoder and prompted alike---has at least one
project it scores 0.000 on and one it scores 1.000 on. Only the middle of the
distribution separates them: the encoders' median per-project accuracy is 0.917
(s.d.\ 0.198) against medians of 0.545--0.750 (s.d.\ 0.213--0.301) for the small
open models. A corpus-level average is a weak predictor of what a practitioner
meets on one project.

\textbf{The mechanism is a shift in class balance.} A drop in score does not by
itself say why a model failed, and the two candidate explanations---unfamiliar
vocabulary and a shifted class prior---imply different remedies. The per-class
evidence separates them (Fig.~\ref{fig:prior}). After transfer from SecReq, BERT
labels 44.2\% of the \pex{} items \textit{security}, against a true prevalence of
12.9\% in those items and 39.9\% in the corpus it was trained on. That 44.2\% is
a predicted class share, not a loss of score, and its closeness to the 42.8\%
above is a coincidence. Its consequence is visible per class: precision on the
security class falls from 0.847 to 0.210 while recall falls far less (0.888 to
0.720). The model still finds the security requirements; it cannot stop finding
them. That is the signature of a shifted prior, not of a model that has failed
to read the text.

The picture is not uniform, and we report it as measured. RoBERTa carries less
of its source prior across (19.7\% predicted against 12.9\% true) and loses
correspondingly less, and in the reverse direction both encoders predict
\emph{below} the target prevalence (33.6\% and 29.1\% against 39.9\%), so content
differences contribute there too. What the evidence supports is that the
dominant term in the largest observed collapse is a prior the model brought with
it. That is a comparatively encouraging diagnosis, since prior shift is
correctable without labels from the target
corpus~\cite{saerens2002,quinonero2009}. Applying such a correction would change
the quantity being measured, so we leave it as the next step.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_prior_shift.pdf}
\caption{One failure mode, two sources. (a) After cross-dataset transfer an
encoder labels items at a rate pulled towards the base rate of the corpus it was
\emph{trained} on. The axis is the share of test items predicted
\textit{security}, not a score. (b) The consequence for the same model:
precision on the security class collapses while recall is largely preserved.
(c) The prompted models show the same defect from another source: on FR/NFR
their accuracy ranks with how far their predicted class share sits from the true
one.}
\label{fig:prior}
\end{figure}

\subsection{One failure mode, two sources}
\label{sec:prior}
Section~\ref{sec:rq2} attributed the encoders' collapse to a prior carried over
from training. Turning the same instrument on the prompted models finds the same
defect there, arriving by a different route.

\emph{Prompted models also mis-set the class balance, and it explains most of
their error.} On FR/NFR the true NFR share is 54.2\%, and every prompted model
predicts NFR less often than that, from 14.9\% (Qwen2.5-3B) to 43.4\%
(Llama-3.3-70B). Their accuracies rank almost exactly with that miscalibration
(Spearman $\rho = 0.95$ over the eight reportable models,
Fig.~\ref{fig:prior}\,(c)), so the small open models' weak FR/NFR scores reflect
a systematic bias towards answering \textsc{fr} rather than an inability to read
the requirement.

\emph{The wording of the question moves that balance directly}, which is what
makes the link causal rather than correlational. Across the nine paired cells of
the phrasing sub-study (Table~\ref{tab:prompt}) the median spread between the
three wordings is 0.044 \Fm{}, but the largest is 0.485, for Gemma-2-2B on
SecReq security. The predictions show what the \emph{terse} wording does: it is
the only variant phrased as a leading yes/no question, and under it Gemma-2-2B
answers \textit{security} for 96.7\% of SecReq and 51.3\% of \pex{} items,
against true rates of 39.7\% and 12.7\% in those frames. Qwen2.5-7B shifts the
same way but less far. This is not a formatting artefact: the strict parser
accepted 99.98\% of the sub-study's 11{,}518 responses, so the answers were
well-formed and simply wrong. Re-wording the question re-set the model's prior
in the same way that re-training on another corpus re-set the encoder's. Prompt
sensitivity of this kind is documented in the prompting
literature~\cite{zhao2021calibrate,lu2022fantastically}; what is new here is
that it lands on the same failure mode as the encoders' transfer loss.

\emph{Few-shot exemplars help where they carry information about the class
balance.} Across the 90 paired comparisons on the six local models---the only
tier that ran few-shot---the median gain is $+0.024$ \Fm{}, but the effect
splits by task: slightly negative on the binary tasks (mean $-0.007$ over 54
comparisons; the 30 BH-significant effects average $-0.027$) and positive on the
sub-types (mean $+0.062$ over 36; all 14 BH-significant effects are gains,
averaging $+0.114$). Where the labels are a familiar convention the model
already has a prior and the examples mostly perturb it, which is the
over-prompting effect Tang et al.\ report~\cite{tang2025}; where they are an
unfamiliar eleven-class taxonomy, the exemplars are the only statement of what
the classes mean.

These are one defect with two sources. The task needs a class prior that cannot
be read off the requirement text, and each family acquires one from somewhere it
should not: the encoder from its training corpus, the prompted model from its
pre-training and from the wording of the question. Neither is calibrated to the
corpus in front of it, which is why neither is safe to deploy on an
in-distribution score alone.

\subsection{RQ3: the accuracy--cost trade-off}
\label{sec:rq3}
Table~\ref{tab:cost} gives cost and latency by tier and Fig.~\ref{fig:cost} the
frontier. Encoder inference costs \$0.0024 per 1{,}000 classifications on the
imputed T4 rental. The prompted configurations range from \$0.0248 to \$0.0704
per 1{,}000 on the same basis, taking each model's median across its cells: 10
to 29 times the encoder, and about 19 times at the medians. One-off fine-tuning
is small---a median of \$0.0093 per deployable model, about 277 GPU-seconds over
all folds of a family---so the break-even of Eq.~\eqref{eq:breakeven} is reached
quickly: over all 276 encoder-versus-alternative pairings $N^{\star}$ lies
between 46 and 552 items, with a median of 215. The Pareto frontier over
reportable cells holds ten cells, nine of them encoders. The one prompted
frontier point is 4-bit Qwen2.5-7B on SecReq security, which is the strongest
freely available option on the one cell where transfer is what is being
measured.

Two qualifications keep these figures in proportion. They are ratios measured on
one machine at one date, and the prices behind them move: list rates change, and
cost within the compute-priced tier scales with model size
(Section~\ref{sec:costmodel}). And the model prices computation only---the human
annotation an encoder needs before it can be fine-tuned is excluded, which
favours the encoder.

Latency behaves differently from cost. The median per-request latency is
0.016\,s for the encoders, 0.095\,s for the hosted 70\,B model, 0.194--0.356\,s
for the local open models and 0.614\,s for the commercial API. Free-tier queueing
inflates the hosted \emph{means} by up to two orders of magnitude, which is why
all wall-clock projections use medians.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_cost.pdf}
\caption{RQ3. (a) SecReq security, the one cell a prompted model leads: 4-bit
Qwen2.5-7B buys $+0.011$ \Fm{} for roughly $19\times$ the cost per item. (b)
Cumulative cost against classified volume; fine-tuning is repaid within 46--552
classifications across all 276 pairings. Both panels use the cost basis of

\label{fig:cost}
\end{figure}

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Discussion}
%% ===========================================================================

\subsection{Generalizability}
The most consequential result here is not that one family is better, but that
the answer to ``which is better?'' changes between two protocols the literature
treats as interchangeable, on the same corpora, the same items and the same
scorer. A benchmark reporting only in-distribution numbers is not a weaker
version of one that reports transfer; on this evidence it can report the
opposite ordering. Two things follow. The regime belongs in the claim, next to
the metric. And ``generalisation'' should mean held-out projects or an
independently annotated corpus, not transfer across tasks within one dataset,
which is what the term currently covers in parts of this
literature~\cite{binkhonain2025}.

The limits of our own claim should be equally explicit. We observe the reversal
on one corpus pair, one task both corpora annotate, and one language. The study
establishes that the reversal is possible and large when it happens, not that it
occurs at any particular rate across requirements corpora. The mechanism we
identify---a class prior carried over from the training corpus---is what would
make it recur, and it can be checked on any new pair without re-running our
models, by comparing the predicted class share against the target prevalence.

\subsection{Consistency and reliability}
Accuracy averaged over a corpus is not the only property a practitioner needs.
Two kinds of instability appear in the results, one in each family.

The encoders are stable given a fixed training distribution and unstable when it
moves: their scores change little across folds within a corpus but lose up to
42.8\% of their in-domain macro-F1 when the training corpus is replaced. Their
failure is at least predictable from something checkable before deployment,
namely the class balance of the corpus they were fitted on relative to the
target.

The prompted models are stable across regimes---by construction, since nothing
is re-fitted---but unstable with respect to the question. Re-wording the same
instruction, with the answer contract held fixed, moved macro-F1 by up to 0.485
in one cell. A deployment that pins its prompt gets repeatable answers, but the
level at which they are repeatable was set by a wording choice no
in-distribution study would surface. Both families also show wide per-project
variance, with every configuration recording at least one project scored 0.000
and one scored 1.000. A corpus-level mean reported without a per-project spread
overstates how reliable either family is in practice.

\subsection{Accuracy--cost trade-off}
For a team with a few hundred labelled requirements from the domain it will
operate in, and any non-trivial volume, a fine-tuned encoder of about 110\,M
parameters is both the more accurate and much the cheaper option, and it repays
its training cost within a few hundred classifications. Entering an unlabelled
or shifting domain changes the answer: a mid-size quantised open model gives up
in-domain accuracy, degrades more gracefully, and runs on one consumer-class GPU
without an API contract. What the results argue against is the implicit default
of much recent work---fine-tuning on one corpus and assuming the result
transfers.

The trade-off is a ratio, not a price. The absolute figures in
Section~\ref{sec:rq3} are tied to one GPU, one date and two rate cards; what
should survive is the order of magnitude between a 110\,M-parameter encoder and
a multi-billion-parameter generative model doing the same classification, and
the fact that within the compute-priced tier cost tracks model size. The
annotation an encoder route needs is real and sits outside the model: a team
without labels is not choosing between two prices per thousand items, it is
choosing between annotating and not.

\subsection{Contamination and availability}
Both corpora are old, small and public, so prompted in-domain scores may be
inflated by pre-training contamination~\cite{sainz2023}. That bias would
overstate the prompted models in-domain, which is where we report the encoders
winning, so the in-domain encoder advantage is conservative; and it cannot
produce the cross-dataset reversal, since it would help the prompted models in
both regimes equally. The pipeline, the frozen splits, the full prediction store
and the scripts that regenerate every table and figure are public. Splits are
hash- and seed-pinned and scoring is a pure function of the stored raw outputs,
so every number here reproduces without re-running a model.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Threats to Validity}
%% ===========================================================================

\textbf{Internal.} The commercial tier ran at about 60 items per cell, where 23
of its 26 paired comparisons are inconclusive, so ``never significantly beaten''
partly reflects limited statistical power. Free-tier quotas caused
missing-not-at-random dropout on some hosted configurations; the reportability
gate excludes the affected cells rather than imputing them. Local models ran
4-bit quantised, which may understate full-precision accuracy, and each
configuration used a single seed, so small encoder-to-encoder margins should not
be over-read.

\textbf{Construct.} GPU costs are imputed from a published rental rate rather
than billed, and token prices are 2026 list rates, so the ratios are more
durable than the absolute values. $N^{\star}$ is a pure cost crossover computed
regardless of the accuracy gap, and the cost model prices computation only, so
the annotation an encoder needs is excluded---which favours the encoder. Strict
scoring counts format non-compliance as error, matching deployment but differing
from the lenient protocols of some prior work. The prompt is fixed by design
(Section~\ref{sec:prompt}); the phrasing sub-study bounds what a better wording
would be worth on two models and nine cells, not on all eight.

\textbf{External.} Both corpora are small, dated and public, and their security
label sets differ: \pex{}'s is derived from the security sub-class and is
non-functional by construction, whereas SecReq annotates any security-relevant
sentence. The cross-dataset regime therefore carries definitional as well as
distributional shift, on one corpus pair. Results cover English requirements and
one NFR taxonomy.

\textbf{Conclusion.} All paired tests are exact and multiplicity-corrected as
one family, and the frozen splits are stored once and never regenerated because
grouped-fold membership is library-version dependent.

%% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
%% ===========================================================================

We compared four fine-tuned encoder configurations against eight prompted LLMs
on three requirements-classification tasks, holding the items, the label sets
and the scoring rule fixed and varying only the distribution shift between what
a model was fitted on and what it was scored on. Within a corpus the encoders
are ahead and are never significantly beaten. Across an independently annotated
corpus the ordering reverses and the prompted models are ahead in most
comparisons, while the encoders remain an order of magnitude cheaper per item.
The cause is the same in both families: a class prior acquired from somewhere
other than the corpus being classified---from the training data in one case,
from the wording of the instruction in the other.

An in-distribution score is therefore not a partial answer to the question of
which approach to adopt; it can be the wrong one. Work in this area should
report the evaluation regime as part of the result, and should treat the
predicted class balance as a diagnostic to check before deployment rather than a
detail of the confusion matrix.
